paras: The Healdton lynchings were the hanging of Bill Morgan and two or three other men by a mob of citizens near Healdton, in the Chickasaw Nation of Indian Territory, on the night of Monday, April 9, 1888. The men were accused of belonging to a band of horse thieves, and federal deputy marshals afterward arrested some of those said to have been in the mob. Newspapers in Texas and across the country carried the news from Gainesville, Texas, and the case was later entered in year-end tallies of lynchings.

Healdton was described as a small village twenty miles northwest of Gainesville. Over the preceding winter, according to the Gainesville wire, a "bold band of horse-thieves" had been stealing large numbers of horses in the Chickasaw Nation, running them into Texas and selling them.

On Monday night, men living near Healdton who were believed to be connected with that band were seized by a mob of local residents and hanged. A separate Gainesville dispatch said three men had been "arrested by a mob of citizens" and hanged a short distance from the village. Only one victim was named, Bill Morgan; the man who carried the news to Gainesville had forgotten the other names, and territory residents who came to the city could not supply them.

Deputy U.S. marshals arrested some of those accused of taking part, and the traveler who brought the news had met two marshals escorting one alleged mob member. Residents of the territory who were in Gainesville confirmed the report and said hangings would continue until horse thieves and other criminals were convinced "that the nation is no longer a harbor for outlaws." No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial of the arrested men appears in the coverage.

A St. Louis Post-Dispatch special from Gainesville appeared on April 12 in papers in Savannah, Memphis, Indianapolis and Emporia, under headlines such as "Horse Thieves Hanged" and "Hanged by Enraged Citizens." That wire called the dead "executed thieves" and their killers "enraged citizens," treating the accusation as established. Texas papers ran their own Gainesville special, which the Fort Worth Gazette headlined "A Triple Lynching" and the Austin Statesman "Judge Lynch. He Holds Court in the Indian Territory," printing the residents' warning of further hangings without comment.

Michigan weeklies reprinted the wire in a regional news column and reduced the story to a single line about horse thieves "strung up by vigilants." In December, year-end lists of "Victims of Judge Lynch" recorded it as "Bill Morgan and three other horsethieves" hanged on April 9. None of the articles stated the race of the victims or of the mob.

The number of dead differs: the first wire gave no figure, the Texas special reported three, and the later Michigan summary and year-end list said four. The figure of three came from a traveler who had spoken with the marshals, while the later lists cite no source for four.

reader.title: Healdton lynchings (1888)
bases: Men accused of belonging to a horse-thief band were seized by a mob of citizens near Healdton and hanged, and some alleged mob members were arrested by federal deputy marshals (A2, A5, A6).

Every account says the men were hanged by a 'mob' of citizens (later 'vigilants'), and several of its members were arrested, so the killing was extralegal and by a group (A2, A6, A9); the stated reason was their alleged link to a band of horse thieves (A5, A7).

Two separate Gainesville dispatches, the Post-Dispatch special (A2, A5) and the Gazette/Statesman special (A6, A7), agree on the hanging near Healdton, the horse-theft accusation, the victim Morgan and the arrests, although they differ on how many died and both rest on second-hand news reaching Gainesville.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special from Gainesville
accounts.gist: Thieves living near Healdton, believed connected with a horse-thief band, were seized Monday night by a mob of local citizens and hanged; one was Bill Morgan; some of the mob were arrested by deputy marshals. No number of dead is given.

accounts.label: Gazette/Statesman special from Gainesville
accounts.gist: Three men were arrested by a mob of citizens and hanged; the news came from a traveler who met two deputy marshals with an alleged mob member in custody; one victim was named Morgan.

accounts.label: Territory citizens in Gainesville
accounts.gist: Confirmed the hangings and said they would continue until horse thieves were convinced the nation was no longer a harbor for outlaws.

accounts.label: Later summaries
accounts.gist: Four horse thieves were strung up by vigilants; a year-end list gives April 9 and 'Bill Morgan and three other horsethieves'.

framing.detail: The Post-Dispatch wire ran under 'Hanged by a Mob', 'HORSE THIEVES HANGED' and 'Horse-Thieves Hanged', calling the dead 'executed thieves' and the mob 'enraged citizens'.
Texas papers headlined 'A TRIPLE LYNCHING' and 'JUDGE LYNCH. He Holds Court in the Indian Territory', and printed the citizens' warning that hangings would continue without comment.
Michigan weeklies reduced it to a one-line item about 'vigilants' and an entry in a year-end 'Victims of Judge Lynch' list.

conflicts.note: The three-victim figure comes from the Gainesville special that relied on a traveler's talk with the marshals; the four-victim figure appears only in later Michigan summaries, which give no source. Neither is clearly better evidence.
